intro: If you run a primary school in Kenya, the [best school management software in Kenya](/blog/best-school-management-software-kenya) is the one that fits *your* learners — not the one built for a boarding secondary school with Form 4 exam analytics you will never use.

Most "primary" schools in Kenya are no longer purely primary. CBC now carries the same learner from Grade 1 to Grade 9, and many schools also run Form 1–4 on 8-4-4. That changes the question from "primary or secondary software?" to "can one system cover both?"
This guide sets out what primary schools actually need, how secondary needs differ, and how to choose software that will still fit when your school grows into — or already runs — a secondary section.

sections.heading: What primary schools in Kenya actually need from software

blocks.text: A Kenyan primary school's needs are narrower — and more specific — than a secondary school's. Three of them decide whether software helps or simply adds another login.

items: **CBC Grade 1–9 assessment.** Rubrics, strands and continuous assessment for young learners, captured as teachers observe them and turned into term reports without retyping.
**Many parents, many small M-Pesa payments.** Primary fees often arrive in frequent, smaller amounts, so matching every Paybill or till payment to the right learner matters even more than the amount.
**Parent communication at primary level.** Absence alerts, homework notices and fee reminders over WhatsApp and SMS, because at this age the school talks to parents constantly.

blocks.text: Secondary features such as Form 4 subject analytics or boarding prep supervision are not wrong — they are simply not what a Grade 1–6 school should pay to carry.

sections.heading: How secondary school needs differ (Form 1–4 under 8-4-4)

blocks.text: Secondary schools under 8-4-4 have different problems, and the difference shows up in three places.

items: **Subject-based grading and exam analytics.** Many subjects, several teachers per subject, and reporting that ranks and compares — mean score, position, and subject strengths and weaknesses.
**Boarding, duty rosters and larger fee structures.** House and prep supervision, duty rosters across staff, and fewer but larger fee payments, often made by instalment.
**Complex timetables.** Streams, shared labs and specialised teachers make the master timetable harder to build than in a primary school.

blocks.text: None of this means a secondary school needs a *different product* — only that the product must handle both sets of needs when a school spans both stages.

sections.heading: Primary vs secondary: what to compare

blocks.text: When you shortlist software, compare it against the needs of your actual stages. The table below summarises where primary (Grade 1–9, CBC) and secondary (Form 1–4, 8-4-4) requirements diverge.

blocks.caption: Primary vs secondary needs at a glance
rows: CBC rubrics, strands and continuous assessment
Subject grades, mean score, position and comments
Fewer, larger payments, often by instalment
WhatsApp and SMS for attendance, homework and fees
WhatsApp and SMS for exams, boarding and fees

blocks.text: The pattern is clear: primary schools need **breadth of parent contact and simple, frequent fees**; secondary schools need **depth in grading and complexity in operations**. A growable school should look for both.

sections.heading: The combined-school problem: Grade 1–9 plus Form 1–4 on one platform

blocks.text: Many Kenyan schools are now **combined**: a primary section running CBC Grade 1–9, and a secondary section running Form 1–4 on 8-4-4. Running one system for the primary section and another for the secondary section means two homes for one school's data.

sections.heading: Why two systems create two versions of the truth

blocks.text: Two systems create two versions of the truth. The parent list drifts apart, the fee balances never agree, and the director's morning question — "how many learners, how much collected, how much outstanding?" — has no single answer.

items: **Duplicate learner records** for siblings, or for a learner who moves between sections.
**Duplicate data entry** for the same staff and the same families.
**No group-level report** for the director or board — just two sets of exports stapled together.

blocks.text: A combined view on one platform removes that reconciliation work entirely, which is why "combined primary and junior secondary software" is fast becoming the real search term for Kenyan head teachers.

sections.heading: Fee collection for primary schools: many parents, many small M-Pesa payments

blocks.text: Primary schools feel M-Pesa pressure differently: hundreds of parents, each paying a small amount, often in more than one instalment. Done by hand, that is hundreds of matches every week of the term.

items: **Matching Paybill and till payments to the right learner.** The account number (ideally the admission number) or the guardian's registered phone identifies the learner automatically, so the balance updates the same day.
**Partial payments and receipts.** Primary fees often arrive in parts; the balance should reflect each payment and issue a receipt each time, not only when the total is cleared.

**Reminders that reflect the real balance.** With live balances, reminders go only to parents who actually owe — see [fee reminder templates for SMS and WhatsApp](/blog/school-fee-reminder-sms-whatsapp-kenya).

blocks.text: For the mechanics, including what happens when a reference is wrong, see [automatic M-Pesa reconciliation for schools](/blog/mpesa-integration-school-management-software-kenya).
At primary level the report card is the artefact parents judge the school by, and it should be both accurate and easy to read.

items: **CBC narrative and rubric report cards** that describe what a learner can do, not only a score — captured as the teacher assesses.
**Print-ready term reports for every level**, in the format each stage requires, produced without retyping a single mark.
**Consistency for parents.** One platform that produces the right report for Grade 1–9 and for Form 1–4 means one standard across the whole school.

blocks.text: For a closer look at the CBC side, see [CBC report card software in Kenya](/blog/cbc-report-card-software-kenya).

sections.heading: What a primary school can leave out — and what it must not

blocks.text: Keeping costs sane is part of choosing well. A primary school can often leave out the heaviest secondary-grade machinery without losing anything it needs today.

items: **Worth skipping, for now:** deep Form 4 subject analytics, boarding house management, and complex multi-stream timetabling — unless you actually run those.
**Non-negotiables:** reliable fee records, automatic M-Pesa reconciliation, WhatsApp and SMS parent messaging, and daily backups with role-based access.
**Grow into it, not out of it:** choose a system whose secondary features are already there, so adding a section later is a setting, not a migration.

blocks.title: Ask before you skip
blocks.text: Confirm that a feature you skip today can be switched on later without a new contract — otherwise "cheaper now" quietly becomes "migrate later".

Attendance alerting sits firmly in the non-negotiable column for primary schools: young learners cannot report their own absence, so [attendance tracking with parent SMS alerts](/blog/student-attendance-tracking-parent-sms) becomes a welfare feature, not a luxury.

faqs.question: Is there software built specifically for Kenyan primary schools?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the more useful question is whether it covers CBC Grade 1–9 *and* a secondary section. SQUL handles both, so a primary school that grows into Grade 9 or adds Form 1–4 does not have to change systems.

faqs.question: Can one system handle both my primary and secondary sections?
faqs.answer: Yes. A system built for both CBC Grade 1–9 and 8-4-4 Form 1–4 keeps one learner record and one fee balance, and gives the director a combined view instead of two sets of exports.

faqs.question: How long does it take a primary school to go live?
faqs.answer: With an existing learner list, most primary schools go live in about two weeks — the main work is importing learners and linking guardian phone numbers for M-Pesa matching and parent messaging.
